1.pericope_label: Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife
debates: What fills the house in the first proverb
Whether the fourth verse describes a profligate or defines one
On what ground mocking the poor reproaches God
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word means sacrificial gifts and take it of slain animals, the old name for the peace offerings, part burnt and part served as a feast
Keil and Delitzsch hold that the clause about false lips does not describe what a profligate does but stamps as a profligate whoever does it
Keil and Delitzsch ground the reproach on creation, since the poor man as poor is the work of God, who appointed him his lowly place
Henry marks the limit of the fining-pot figure, that men may try silver but have no way of trying one another hearts
themes: Holy love found in a cottage
A servant taken in for a child share
A metal both proved and improved
A cup put into the hand that was glad to see it filled

6.pericope_label: Children of children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers
debates: Which man the gift is a jewel to
What the key word of the seventh proverb means
Whether the traditional text of the tenth needs correcting
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch derive the rank of inherited nobility from the second half of the sixth verse, since a man may abnegate his social rights and still remain part of the moral order
Keil and Delitzsch reject three renderings of the key word and settle on presumptuous, properly words of superfluity and high pretension
Keil and Delitzsch argue that the person and not the gift must be the subject of the second clause, since the verb is used only of persons
Wesley enters a caution that this proverb, like many others in the book, is to be understood of most men and not of all
themes: A crown made of grandchildren
Fine words as unbecoming as a cart wheel among clockwork
A great bell not struck when a neighbour sins
A word enough for one man and stripes too little for another

11.pericope_label: An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him
debates: Which word is subject in the eleventh proverb
What the last phrase of the fourteenth means
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch take rebellion as the subject, an abstract standing for a concrete, since seeking after evil is a more natural connection of ideas than seeking after rebellion
Keil and Delitzsch grade the offence, placing ingratitude among the manifestations of ignoble selfishness and the returning of evil for good far above it
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both render the last phrase of the fourteenth as before the showing of teeth, a metaphor from an angry dog
Keil and Delitzsch observe that acquitting the guilty seems the milder fault than condemning the innocent, and that the proverb makes both alike an abhorrence
themes: A messenger read as a sergeant, an executioner and an angel
Folly morbidly heightened into madness
A dam torn away rather than a tap opened
A distinction confounded by private men as well as judges

16.pericope_label: Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no heart to it?
debates: Whether the neighbour in the suretyship proverb is the creditor or the debtor
Whether the exalted gate is a doorway or the mouth
What the price in the hand of the fool stands for
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch make the sixteenth verse one question and not two, and deny that the preposition can mean on behalf of
Clarke prefers to read the gate as the mouth and its exalting as arrogant speech, judging that this suits the context better than a literal doorway
Ellicott holds that a man may pay high for instruction and still remain a fool if he has no capacity for taking it in
Henry warns that generosity to a friend must not become injustice to a family
themes: Swallow-friends who fly to you in summer and are gone in winter
Doors kept under three feet so that horsemen cannot ride in
An old saying that whoever busies himself with building grows poor
A house and estate going out at the gate

21.pericope_label: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones
debates: Whether the rare word in the twenty-second means medicine or body
Whether the fool seeks wisdom in the wrong place or keeps nothing in view at all
Whether the sorrow of the twenty-first is a purpose or a consequence
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject the ancient versions that render the rare word body, since another word is used for that, while Clarke accepts the variant as making the halves answer each other exactly
Keil and Delitzsch prefer, from the order of the words, that wisdom lies before the understanding as his aim rather than that he finds it everywhere
Gill insists the fool of the twenty-first is not an idiot but a wicked son
Henry insists the giver of a bribe is as bad as the taker
themes: A gift passed under four eyes
A purse carried in the bosom above the girdle
Wisdom laid out as a card and compass
Mirth prescribed sparingly and by rule

25.pericope_label: He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit
debates: What the opening particle of the twenty-sixth attaches to
Whether the excellent spirit means sparing of words or weighty and composed
Whether striking a ruler is ever warranted
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject three readings of the opening particle and insist the proverb must have a meaning complete in itself
Keil and Delitzsch prefer a weighty spirit, a quiet seriousness maintaining itself in self-control, over the gloss of a spirit held back
Clarke holds that taking off the head of a ruler under pretence of his not being equitable is a dreadful omen to any land
Henry divides the pain of a foolish son between anger in the father and bitterness in the mother
themes: Silence called the covering of the stupid
A cool head with a warm heart
Knowing when to be silent called better than diamonds
Parents told to comfort each other under a common grief
